source: Equilibrium and the First Law
Zero net force means constant velocity, and standing still is the special case where that velocity is zero.
Students think an object moving at constant speed needs a net force in its direction of motion.

Newton's First Law: Inertia said an object keeps its velocity unless a net force acts. With Free-Body Diagrams, that becomes a tool: whenever the velocity is constant, the forces on the diagram must add to zero.

Equilibrium means $\Sigma \vec{F} = 0$, which happens exactly when the velocity is constant: at rest, or moving in a straight line at a steady speed. In components: $\Sigma F_x = 0$ and $\Sigma F_y = 0$.

A net force changes velocity; that is what the second law says. So if the velocity isn't changing, there is no net force, whatever the speed. A car cruising at $30\ \text{m/s}$ on a straight road is in equilibrium just as much as a parked car: the forward force from the road exactly balances drag and rolling friction.
A pushed cart with friction. Balanced forces keep its speed steady; they don't stop it.
Worked examples
You push a $40\ \text{kg}$ crate across a floor at a constant velocity with a $120\ \text{N}$ horizontal push. How big is the friction force?
Constant velocity
Constant velocity: $\Sigma F_x = 0$.
$120 - f = 0$, so $f = 120\ \text{N}$. The mass isn't needed.
An elevator car of mass $800\ \text{kg}$ rises at a steady $2\ \text{m/s}$. What is the cable's tension?
Moving, yet balanced
Steady velocity, so $\Sigma F_y = 0$: $T - mg = 0$.
$T = (800)(9.8) = 7{,}840\ \text{N}$, the same as if it were parked.

Thinking an object moving at a constant speed needs a net force in its direction of motion. That idea fits everyday life, where friction stops things, but the extra push only cancels friction. Check: is the velocity changing? If not, the net force is zero, and the forward forces equal the backward ones.
